To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the surface functionalization of a continuously moving polypropylene film in a repetitively pulses atmospheric pressure discharge can be optimized by controlling the gas composition, residence time, and the relative abundance of short-lived and long-lived species.
the functional groups on a polypropylene surface can be tailored by varying the gas flow rate and pulse frequency.
the functionalization of a polymer film in an atmospheric pressure corona discharge is a complex process that is influenced by the local plasma chemistry, gas flow and surface reactions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of computational models to investigate the fundamental chemistry and physics of the plasma–polymer interaction.
understanding the fundamental chemistry of plasma processing of polymers.

the development of a fundamental understanding of the complex chemistry that occurs in these systems, which is necessary to optimize the surface functionalization and to develop a new generation of atmospheric plasma processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the surface chemistry of the polymer in this process is complex and depends on the interplay of local and non-local reactions.
a combination of gas composition, flow velocity and residence time can be used to optimize the functionalization of the polymer sheet.
the discharge and surface chemistry are coupled in a complex manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the plasma chemistry is complex and the surface processing is highly non-local.

the surface chemistry and functional group distributions are determined by the balance between the local chemistry of the gas phase, the residence time of species in the discharge zone and the non-local chemistry of the gas and surface.

the surface chemistry of a polymer sheet in an atmospheric pressure pulsed discharge can be controlled by adjusting the gas composition, the gas flow rate, the discharge power, and the pulse repetition frequency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the discharge zone and inter-pulse period should be considered in concert to understand the plasma–surface chemistry.
, for the same average power, a high pulse repetition frequency (PRF) is more efficient in generating reactive fluxes than a low PRF.
the gas flow and residence time in the discharge zone can be exploited to control the relative abundance of reactive species in the gas phase and the surface functional groups on the polymer.
